title: Rate comparison: FF density-zero failures (Thm 5.3) vs Vaughan's exceptional-set bound
connection: At fixed q the FF failures have density 0 via a one-prime identity plus Dirichlet/RH in F_q[T]; over Z Vaughan gives #exceptions ≤ N exp(−c log^{2/3} N). The FF proof uses RH (Weil), so its rate may be a power saving.
why: A power-saving rate in FF suggests what GRH would buy over Z; a GRH-conditional power-saving ES exceptional bound would be a new (conditional) integer theorem.
first_step: Extract the explicit rate in FUNCTIONFIELD_ES Thm 5.3; then check whether a GRH-conditional ES exceptional-set bound with power saving exists in the literature (search 'Erdős–Straus exceptional set GRH').
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Squares in F_q[T] are not obstructed: compute ES at P = Q² to see what 'unobstructed squares' look like
connection: FF has no T1 at squares (odd q), so ES_q(A, Q²) is solved by ordinary certificates. Comparing the certificate types used at FF squares vs non-squares shows which Z certificates would be needed at odd squares.
why: Z's odd squares are known ES-true but certificate-line-empty; the FF certificates at squares are a template for what a 'non-line' solution at a Z square looks like.
first_step: For q = 3, A = T, list solutions at P = Q², deg Q ≤ 4, classify by Type I/II and certificate line; compare with Z solutions at 25, 49, 121.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Totally positive ES for non-rational n ∈ Z[√3]: every class of (O_K/4)^* covered (EVIDENCE)
connection: other_rings found that for D = 3, 6 every class is hit, so positive ES holds for every totally positive n ∈ O_K prime to 2. That is a full ES theorem in a ring with infinite units.
why: Proves ES-for-all-n in a non-trivial ring; checking whether the proof is a finite covering by unit identities gives a template.
first_step: Extract from bs_ff_rings.py output the explicit list of (η, κ) identities covering each class and package as a theorem with proof.

title: ES over F_q (finite fields) with a 'size' notion via lifting to [0, q): box-restricted solutions
connection: Over F_q, 4/n = Σ 1/x_i trivially has solutions. Requiring representatives x_i ∈ [1, H] with H small (a box) gives the 'small solutions of congruences' world (Heath-Brown, Shparlinski style).
why: ES at p ⇔ an integer solution, but a box-solution modulo a suitable modulus M with box H < M^{1/3}-ish lifts automatically; small-solution theorems for multiplicative congruences might give partial results.
first_step: Formulate: for M = p·(something), does 4xyz ≡ p(xy+yz+zx) mod M with x,y,z ≤ M^θ force equality? Then search the literature for small solutions of such congruences.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Meta: catalogue of 'verified to 10^N, then false' small-count conjectures
connection: Collect conjectures with small expected counts that failed only at large N (Pólya 9·10^8, Mertens, Skewes, Euler sum of powers) and compare their count regimes with ES.
why: All large-first-counterexample examples are oscillation/structure-driven, not count-driven; ES verification to 10^18 is strong evidence against random-type failures but not structural ones.
first_step: Tabulate (expected count at first failure, mechanism) for each; check whether any count-driven conjecture failed beyond 10^9.

title: 9/n fails exactly at {2,5,11,19} (≤ 10⁵ primes, n ≤ 4000)
connection: Tiny, apparently complete exception set for 9/n; 9 = 3² so 9/n relates to 3/n-type identities.
why: Small complete exception lists are the most 'fingerprintable'; no OEIS hit for {2,5,11,19} beyond spurious ones.
first_step: Prove completeness of {2,5,11,19} for 9/n by covering congruences (expected possible since 9/n has many identities) — a warm-up for the ES covering obstruction.

title: ES count at odd squares is normal: U(m²)/median(neighbours) has median 0.92
connection: For odd m ≤ 173, U(m²) is typical (median ratio 0.92, mean 2.5 because m² with smooth m has huge counts: U(225) = 317, U(441) = 491), although every certificate line vanishes at odd squares (T1).
why: Certificate lines see none of the solutions at odd squares, yet the total count there is typical — at m² the solutions come from the composite structure (not all are scalings of 4/m solutions: (4, 6, 36) solves 4/9 but is not a scaled solution of 4/3); a proof via lines must route squares through factors.
first_step: Classify the solutions of 4/m² by whether they are scaled solutions of 4/d for some d | m², d < m², and measure the non-inherited fraction.

title: Denominator gcd stratification
connection: Partition ES triples by the three pairwise denominator gcds and compare the strata with multiplicative parametrizations.
why: The cleared equation 4xyz=p(xy+xz+yz) imposes exact constraints on every gcd stratum.
first_step: Derive the cleared equation after writing x=ga and y=gb with gcd(a,b)=1.

title: Formal translation between word and fraction certificates
connection: Specify both sides of one short matrix-word equivalence and prove the conversion including sign and congruence conditions.
why: A checked bridge would allow discovery in one language and validation in another.
first_step: Select a length-two or length-three word and manually derive the forward and reverse formulas before formalizing.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Optics: thin-lens equation 1/f = 1/u + 1/v as Egyptian fractions
connection: Unit-fraction sums appear in lens/mirror equations; 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is three cascaded optical elements with integer focal lengths. Integer-focal-length lens combinatorics (Gaussian lens formula over ℤ) is a tiny literature.
why: Could supply a geometric (ray-transfer matrix, SL₂(ℤ)) model of unit-fraction sums that matches the known SL₂-word reformulation of ES.
first_step: Write the ray-transfer matrices of three thin lenses with focal lengths x,y,z in contact and compare with the SL₂ word form of ES (FRONTIER §1 'SL₂ words'); search 'integer focal lengths unit fractions'.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0146] Write a short outreach note 'three lenses for every prime' for recreational audiences (cheap community lever).

title: Erdős's own heuristic for ES in 'Some unconventional problems in number theory' and his 'Sierpiński 5/n' remark
connection: Erdős (and Sierpiński for 5/n, Schinzel for a/n with n ≥ n₀(a)) framed the conjecture; Schinzel's generalisation 'a/n in 3 unit fractions for n ≥ n₀(a)' is the natural family. Tools that handle ALL a simultaneously may be forced to use structure invisible for a = 4.
why: The a-family (a/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n ≥ n₀(a)) is a 2-parameter problem; results for specific a (Sierpiński 5/n verified far; Palamà, Yamamoto for a ≤ 36?) and their methods are a direct lead library.
first_step: Search 'Schinzel conjecture a/n three unit fractions n_0(a)' and compile the status table for a ≤ 40 (who proved what, by which identities); check whether any a-value was handled by a non-covering argument.

title: Fermat's descent / Vieta jumping on U_n via the 'swap two coordinates' and 'reflect in the third' involutions
connection: U_n: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx). Solving for z: z = nxy/(4xy − n(x+y)); not a quadratic in z, so no Vieta involution in z directly. But in the homogenised cubic surface there may be involutions via lines on the surface (a cubic surface has 27 lines; the lines through a rational point give conic-bundle involutions).
why: Conic-bundle structure on the cubic surface U_n gives a fibration whose fibres are conics; integral points on conics over ℤ are classical (Legendre); a 'descent along conic fibres' is an ES-specific tool not yet tried? (git grep conic).
first_step: Find the 27 lines of the projective closure of U_n (it's singular, so fewer); pick a conic bundle; write the conic over ℚ(t) and the integrality condition; test for p = 1009 whether integer points lie on few conic fibres.

title: Games: ES as a two-player game (Adversary picks p, Prover picks C, Adversary reveals factorisation...) and its game value
connection: Formulate the proof search as a game to apply game-theoretic/learning-theoretic bounds: Prover's strategy = a (possibly adaptive) sequence of C's; Adversary = the integers. The minimal 'strategy depth' is C_min's worst case.
why: Meta-reformulation; it frames adaptive strategies (choose next C based on factorisation of 4C₁p+1) which are not covering systems — the adaptive route has been underexplored.
first_step: Design an adaptive strategy: C₁ = 1; if 4p+1 = Π q_i (all ≡ 1 mod 4), set C₂ = q₁ (a prime factor), check 4q₁p+1; etc. Test whether adaptive depth is smaller than C_min for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: ES as 'every p has an odd character χ mod 4C and a divisor a of 4Cp+1 with χ(a) = −1 for ALL odd χ' — the character-theoretic restatement of a ≡ −1 (mod 4C)
connection: a ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟺ χ(a) = χ(−1) for all characters χ mod 4C ⟺ χ(a) = −1 for odd χ and +1 for even χ. So the C-form asks for a divisor whose character vector equals that of −1. The 'subgroup relaxation' keeps only one odd character; the full condition is ALL characters. Framing: find (C, a) with χ(a) = χ(−1) ∀χ — a 'complete set of character conditions', the number of which grows with C (φ(4C) conditions), while the number of divisors grows like τ(4Cp+1) ≈ log p on average — the expected number of hits is τ/φ(4C), and Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C) ≈ log p · Σ 1/C → log p · log X. (Same count as before, now seen as 'characters vs divisors'.)
why: The character view suggests a *Fourier-analytic* route: #certificates at C = (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ(−1) Σ_{a | N} χ(a); the χ = trivial term is τ(N)/φ(4C) > 0; the other terms are 'noise' Σ_{a|N} χ(a) = Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e). A certificate fails to exist iff the noise exactly cancels the main term. Average over C of the noise — can it be shown to be o(main) at fixed p? That's the M_BM program (B3 says the average main term is only log²p). Record the restatement.
first_step: Write the exact identity and compute, for p = 409 and C ≤ 1000, main vs noise per C to see HOW cancellation happens (is it via single-prime N = q with χ(q) = +1 for all odd χ — i.e. q ≡ 1-type — or via multi-factor cancellations?).

title: Elsholtz's k-term results: sums of k unit fractions with k ≥ 4 and m/n
connection: Elsholtz (Trans. AMS 2001) 'Sums of k unit fractions' gives lower bounds on solution counts for m/n with k terms ↔ ES k = 3.
why: The k = 4 exceptional set may be provably empty for fixed m with large n by thick-reservoir arguments; seeing why k=3 is not reachable sharpens the barrier.
first_step: Check whether 'm/n = sum of 4 unit fractions for all large n' is proved for each fixed m (and which method), via Elsholtz 2001.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Mock modular / indefinite theta (Zwegers) for the two-sign hyperbola count
connection: Counts of lattice points in hyperbolic regions with sign conditions are coefficients of indefinite theta series. Zwegers completes these to non-holomorphic modular objects. ES₅ counts points on XY = tp+1 in a cone with a character.
why: Indefinite theta series are the natural home of 'divisor counts with sign' (e.g. Hecke's indefinite theta, Andrews–Dyson–Hickerson). Size log²n is consistent with mock objects of weight 1 (σ₀-type).
first_step: For fixed C, write the generating function Σ_{u,B≥1} q^{4CuB−u−B} and test whether it is a known mock theta / Appell–Lerch sum.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0104] Write Σ_n N₋(n) qⁿ as an indefinite theta series of signature (1,1) or (2,2) with a character; check the Zwegers/Vignéras convergence conditions.

title: m/(kp) family: ES(p) ⟸ (4k)/(kp) three-term solutions with k | x,y,z
connection: Generalising: 4/p = 4k/(kp); three-term representations of 4k/(kp) with all denominators divisible by k are exactly ES(p) solutions scaled — so no gain; but representations of (4k+j)/(kp) − j/(kp) mix.
why: Mostly a sanity item: shows trivial transports are tautological; identifies the non-tautological ones (where denominators share only part of k).
first_step: Characterise algebraically when a solution of 4/(kp) yields one of 4/p (gcd conditions) and enumerate non-trivial transports for k ≤ 12.

title: Covering by quadratic-character conditions: ES(p) ⟸ some explicit Legendre-symbol pattern of p
connection: F_q forcing lines ((q/p) = −1 ⟹ ES(p)) known for q ∈ {3,5,7} ↔ multi-symbol patterns (e.g. (3/p)=(5/p)=…=1 ⟹ ?).
why: Hard primes have all small q as QRs; question is the joint distribution; a theorem 'ES(p) if p is a QNR mod some q ≤ Q' + Burgess-like least-QNR bound p^{small} doesn't finish but an explicit 'all q ≤ 13 QR' class is where difficulty concentrates.
first_step: From repo EXSET_CHAR_FORCING.md, list proven forcing lines; compute fraction of primes ≤ 10⁹ not covered by them as a function of n₂(p).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Erdős Problem #242 page and its forum/issue threads as a community channel
connection: erdosproblems.com lists ES as Problem 242 ↔ repo findings (T1 dictionary, BM main term, I3_𝒞) could be posted as remarks/partial results.
why: Problem pages attract the active AI+Lean community; precise 'what is known / what fails' notes prevent duplicated effort and invite targeted help on sub-problems.
first_step: Read erdosproblems.com/242 and its comments; draft a short factual comment listing the repo's sharpest PROVED/CERTIFIED items with pointers (subject to user approval before posting).

title: Bounded gaps (Zhang–Maynard) technology for 'consecutive shifts all constrained' — upper bound on (★)-failures
connection: Upper-bound sieves for simultaneous multiplicative constraints on p+1,…,p+K ↔ #(★)-failures ≤ X ≪ X/(log X)^{1+Σδ_B} (heuristic upper bound becomes theorem via Selberg sieve).
why: A rigorous upper bound on (★)-failures (as a sieve upper bound) is achievable and new? It's an exceptional-set bound for (★) alone — compare with repo's ES exceptional set exponent (3/4); (★) alone can't beat Linnik-type phenomena but upper bound sieve is fine.
first_step: Write the Selberg upper-bound sieve for primes p ≤ X with p+B class-constrained for all B ≤ K and compute the resulting bound as K → ∞ with X.

title: 4/p via 4/p = 1/p + 3/p and 3-term ES for 3/p with one term forced: ES ⟸ 3/p = 1/y + 1/z with p | …
connection: Taking x = p gives 3/p = 1/y + 1/z which by Rav needs divisors d₁+d₂ ≡ 0 mod 3 of p·k — fails for p ≡ 1 mod 3 often ↔ the 'x = p·t' slices (Type I) generalise.
why: Sanity item showing Type I slices are '(4t−1)/(pt) as a 2-term sum'; each t a binary problem with Rav criterion — exact per-t criterion via divisors of p·t·…
first_step: Write the Rav criterion for (4t−1)/(pt) and compute the per-t success probability vs t; compare with Type I counts.

title: Kummer-theory view of the class gate: −1 as product of factor classes ⟺ splitting in a ray class field
connection: d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) for d | N ⟺ the Artin symbol of the ideal (d) in ℚ(ζ_{4C}) equals complex conjugation ↔ ES Type II asks: does 4Cp+1 have a divisor whose Frobenius in Gal(ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ) is complex conjugation?
why: Rephrases the class gate in Galois terms: 'some divisor of N_C has Frobenius = complex conjugation in the 4C-th cyclotomic field' — a Chebotarev-type event for divisors of a single integer; complex conjugation being the target ties nicely to positivity (the real place).
first_step: Write the condition for the d-part using ideals of ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺ (real subfield): d ≡ −1 means d's Frobenius is trivial in the real subfield and nontrivial in ℚ(ζ_{4C}) — split completely in ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺ but not in ℚ(ζ_{4C}). Test whether this suggests using the real cyclotomic field's units.

title: Interval version: every interval [X, X + (log X)^A] contains a prime with a certificate of size ≤ (log X)^B (provable?)
connection: Weak 'short-interval almost-everywhere' statement ↔ provable by first-moment counting if primes in short intervals were available — they're not at polylog length; restate with integers instead of primes.
why: Calibrates exactly which weak pointwise-in-intervals statements are provable; an integer (not prime) version may be elementary.
first_step: Prove: every interval [X, X + H] with H = (log X)^A contains an integer n ≡ 1 mod 4 with ES(n) via a small certificate (e.g. via n ≡ −u mod 4uC−1 for small fixed (u,C) — CRT gives density, so trivially yes for H ≥ 4uC−1). Record that it's trivial for integers and impossible-to-state for primes at this length.

title: Waring's problem: G(3) and the finite exceptional sets (23, 239 need 9 cubes)
connection: ∀n statements with finite explicit exception lists (F25), proved via circle method + explicit computation; 'every large n is a sum of 4 cubes' open (count polylog-ish? no — n^{1/3}).
why: Sums of 4 cubes: almost-all known (Davenport), pointwise open, count ≍ n^{1/3} — a sibling for calibrating ES programs.
first_step: Inspect the proof of the nine-cubes exceptions 23 and 239; test whether the descent step has any reciprocal analogue for 4/p.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0099] List which ES-program steps would, mutatis mutandis, prove 'every large n is a sum of 4 cubes' (calibration).
refs: L. E. Dickson, All integers except 23 and 239 are sums of eight cubes, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 45 (1939) 588–591

title: Loughran–Mitankin / Colliot-Thélène–Wei–Xu: Markoff integral HP and strong approximation
connection: LM count Markoff surfaces x²+y²+z²−xyz = m failing integral HP via BM; CTWX do the BM analysis; both are the Markoff analogues of BL's ES paper.
why: ES and Markoff share the Cayley-cubic geometry (k=4 Markoff closure); Markoff's extra Vieta group action is the key difference.
first_step: Tabulate BM/Hasse statements for Markoff vs ES side by side and identify which Markoff proof steps use the Vieta group.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0147] Check the exact Loughran–Mitankin theorem, then test whether failed ES primes cluster on finitely many thin polynomial orbits.
refs: Loughran–Mitankin, Integral Hasse principle and strong approximation for Markoff surfaces, IMRN (2021), arXiv:1807.10223
https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.10223 (Loughran–Mitankin, Integral Hasse principle and strong approximation for Markoff surfaces)

title: Euclidean-ring extensions and function-field ES
connection: The extension in arXiv:2410.05030 to polynomial rings and other Euclidean rings matches ES F26/F10/F16: it offers a neighboring setting where divisor-class searches may be more tractable.
why: A function-field analogue can expose whether the divisor reformulation has a structural proof independent of integer prime distribution.
first_step: Specialize the algorithm to Z[T] and formulate the polynomial analogue of the ES divisor condition; check which steps use ordering/sign changes unavailable over finite fields.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Two-term failure versus three-term ES threshold
connection: The two-for-two rewriting operator of arXiv:2003.13229 acts on unit-fraction decompositions, matching ES F12/F14/F27; it can be used to probe the term-count transition (two terms fail, three conjecturally suffice).
why: The paper itself proves no two-term obstruction theorem. Applying its rewrite to ES pairs may still show which arithmetic freedom the third ES denominator supplies.
first_step: Use the paper's rewrite relation to characterize when two reciprocal terms can replace a pair in ES, then identify the invariant that prevents a universal two-term reduction.

title: Problem 321: distinctness range for reciprocal sums
connection: Problem 321 ↔ ES F04, F12, F14, F21: multiplicity of reciprocal sums, symmetry and distinct-term constraints.
why: The problem bounds how long reciprocal sums stay distinct, bearing on collisions among candidate ES triples and multiplicity estimates.
first_step: Compare its bounds with the count of ordered versus unordered ES triples; identify whether a collision argument improves a lower bound for R(p).

title: Explicit parametrization rather than mere existence for a cubic form
connection: A025052 gives explicit formulas for x,y,z after writing N=mn² and splitting according to n relative to m+1 and a residue k mod m+1. It matches F13/F15/F16w/F32: an integral surface is solved by casework and short parameters.
why: ES has many sufficient identities but comparatively less unified coverage; this suggests assembling a finite set of parameterized formulas with an explicit remainder case.
first_step: Adapt the three A025052 case splits as a design pattern for ES: choose an integer parameter, reduce to its residue modulo a linear function, and check whether the remainder becomes an integral positive third denominator.

title: Boundary-inclusive representation count changes the exceptional set
connection: A093670 counts unique ab+ac+bc representations with 1≤a≤b≤c, unlike A093669's strict inequalities. It shares F13/F14/F25 and flips the boundary convention, showing that allowing coincident coordinates changes which values have a unique witness.
why: ES parametrizations often rely on distinctness assumptions only for convenience; tracking boundary strata separately can expose missed or degenerate certificates.
first_step: Split ES solutions into all-distinct, exactly-two-equal, and all-equal denominator triples and verify whether any attempted reduction discards a necessary boundary stratum.

title: Markov uniqueness: Vieta jumping on a cubic surface
connection: Markov uniqueness shares F13,F14,F38,F23: integral points on a cubic surface have coordinate permutations and Vieta involutions, with finite computation testing uniqueness. ES is also a cubic surface with S₃ symmetry and involution structure.
why: The Markov descent tree is a direct analogue to investigate for ES: can involutions move a solution toward a canonical small representative or generate families?
first_step: Read the Markov mutation/Vieta descent and explicitly derive any analogous involution of 4/n=1/x+1/y+1/z preserving positive integral points.

title: Quaternion orders and representation of primes
connection: Quaternionic representation problems share F29, F31, F36 and encode prime splitting through lattice or order structure.
why: The Gaussian/quaternion reformulation may give a geometric parametrisation of the hard split-prime classes.
first_step: Write the ES quadratic-form reformulation explicitly and compare its lattice with norm representations in a quaternion order.

title: Slice-rank of the ES 'certificate tensor' modulo q
connection: The cap-set proof bounds sets avoiding a pattern via the slice rank of the pattern's indicator tensor. Consider the tensor T(u, B, C) = 1[4uBC − u − B ≡ p (mod q)] over F_q³; its slice rank bounds how large a product set of parameter values can avoid certificates mod q.
why: Gives polynomial-method bounds on 'certificate-avoiding parameter sets' mod q, a local statement with sharp constants.
first_step: Compute the slice rank (or a polynomial-method upper bound) of T for small q and compare with the largest avoiding product sets found by search.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0069] Compute the slice rank of T_n(x,y,z) = 1[4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)] over 𝔽_ℓ for small ℓ and compare with the size of solution-free sets.
refs: arXiv:1605.01506 (Croot-Lev-Pach, Progression-free sets in Z_4^n are exponentially small)
Ellenberg–Gijswijt, On large subsets of F_q^n with no three-term arithmetic progression, Ann. Math. 185 (2017)

title: Elsholtz-style generalised windmills for x² + ny² as templates for ES windmills
connection: Zagier's one-sentence proof generalises (Elsholtz; Jackson et al.) to involution proofs that primes in certain classes are represented by x² + 2y², x² + 3y², etc. These are verified parity proofs for 'one representation exists' at primes in classes.
why: These are the closest proved windmill-type pointwise theorems. Their combinatorial skeleton (sets of triples with linear involutions) is the template that WINDMILL/INVOLUTION_ES look for, so the known catalogue tells what forms are reachable.
first_step: Collect the known windmill proofs (x² + ny², n ∈ {1,2,3,…}) and their set definitions; check whether the ES Type II data (4abd = pe + 1) can be fitted to any of their shapes.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0285] Search computationally for involutions on finite ES-related sets (e.g. bounded certificate tuples) whose fixed-point count is odd exactly when p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and not a square.
[upgrades-0281] Read the paper; list the equations handled (x² + ky², etc.) and try its windmill construction on the (★) set or on {(u,B,C) : 4uBC − u − B = p}.
refs: Elsholtz, A combinatorial approach to sums of two squares and related problems (2010; check)
Zagier, A one-sentence proof that every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) is a sum of two squares, Amer. Math. Monthly 97 (1990)
Elsholtz, A combinatorial approach to sums of two squares and related problems (2010)

title: Goldbach-type circle method for I3? The minor arcs for tuv − u − v
connection: The circle method treats additive representations. I3 is multiplicative-additive (tuv − u − v), so its exponential-sum generating function Σ e(α(tuv−u−v)) factors through divisor sums. The major arcs give the local density (Haar survival).
why: It gives the analytic-NT native attempt and shows the minor-arc problem is like the ternary divisor problem in progressions (d₃ in APs), which has level of distribution results (Friedlander–Iwaniec, Heath-Brown).
first_step: Write the singular series for I3 and compare with I3_DEEP's Haar survival; record the minor-arc bound needed for a pointwise result (polylog main term ⇒ impossible).

title: Hyperbolic orbifold coverings: Riemann–Hurwitz between ES triangle orbifolds of different n
connection: If S²(x,y,z) covers S²(x′,y′,z′) with degree d, then χ scales: (4/n − 1) = d(4/n′ − 1). Orbifold coverings between triangle orbifolds (Singerman's list of inclusions of triangle groups) therefore give transport between n and n′.
why: Singerman's classification of triangle-group inclusions is finite and explicit, which might give a small set of exact transport laws.
first_step: From Singerman's list, derive all relations n ↦ n′ induced by inclusions Δ(x,y,z) ⊂ Δ(x′,y′,z′); check whether any maps primes to primes.
refs: Singerman, Finitely maximal Fuchsian groups (J. LMS 1972)

title: Integer-coefficient Ehrhart-type identity for the I3 count via negative continuants (Euler's continuant polynomials)
connection: Negative continuants K(b₁,…,b_k) are polynomials (Euler continuants with signs), and the I3/ES₅ word counts are counts of integer points on K = n. Euler's continuant identities (the 'Euler–Minding' rules) give transformations between continuants that might yield bijections between words of different n.
why: Continuant identities are exact. For length 3, K(v,t,u)K(t) − K(v,t)K(t,u) = −1 is exactly AA* = tp + 1 (checked). For longer words (the λ(p) ≤ L ladder), Euler–Minding identities give the analogous factorisations K(middle)·p + 1 = (left)(right), i.e. the level structure of length-L certificates.
first_step: Write the length-4 and length-5 analogues of AA* = tp + 1 via Euler–Minding (e.g. K(a,b,c,d)K(b,c) − K(a,b,c)K(b,c,d) = −1) and read off the 'level' and divisor-class condition for ES-type certificates at length L.

title: Kloosterman refinement in the level variable t for Σ_t D_t^−(tp+1)
connection: Kloosterman's refinement made 4-variable forms work by averaging Kloosterman sums over the Farey denominators. The all-level ES count Σ_t D_t^−(tp+1) is a divisor problem whose Fourier expansion in t produces Kloosterman sums (cf. the Type I Heegner/Kuznetsov note).
why: Kuznetsov is already used for the Type I sum; applying it to the level sum at fixed p is the pointwise version.
first_step: Write Σ_{t≤T} D_t^−(tp+1) via additive characters, identify the Kloosterman sums S(m,n;c), and estimate their contribution using Weil + Kuznetsov for fixed p.

title: Special-function positivity (Askey–Gasper) for weighted ES counts
connection: de Branges reduced every n to the Askey–Gasper positivity of Jacobi-polynomial sums. Seek weights w_C on levels such that Σ_C w_C · D_C(p) is expressible as a positive combination of 'basis' quantities via a classical positivity identity (e.g. Fejér kernels, Jacobi sums), valid for all p.
why: Every-n positivity theorems often reduce to one special-function inequality; ES weighted counts have explicit Fourier expansions over characters.
first_step: Write the character expansion of Σ_C w_C D_C(p) and search for weights making the coefficient vector positive-definite (Bochner/Fejér-type), at least in a model where p's character values are free.

title: Zero-free region analogue: a range of levels where no 'conspiracy' is possible
connection: Linnik's theorem uses a zero-free region near s = 1 for all characters of modulus ≤ Q. For ES, find a range of small levels (C ≤ C₀(p)) where the relevant characters (mod 4C) are so few that a full conspiracy against certificates would force p into explicit square-like residue classes (contradiction for non-squares).
why: Small levels have few characters; a 'no conspiracy at small levels' lemma would be the ES zero-free region.
first_step: For C ≤ 30, characterise the residues of p (mod lcm(4C)) for which all these levels fail; compute the density of such residues and whether they are squares.
